name: Coral Red
lede: Coral red is a warm orange-red named for the skeleton of a reef animal, a hue the books treat mostly as a color word rather than a material.

sections.title: What the name means
sections.body: Paterson's dictionary glosses coral red as a bright red or a deep pink, and old coral as red-orange, so the books themselves disagree on where coral sits between red and pink [1]. This swatch is a moderate reddish orange, about 5.4 units from the ISCC-NBS block of that name, and it carries older names too: Ridgway's 1886 *Nomenclature of Colors* and the RAL system of 1927 both list a coral red [2]. The Google Books record shows the phrase peaking in the 1940s and rising fastest in the 1870s [2].

sections.title: The animal behind the color
sections.body:
The *Pigment Compendium* has an entry for coral, a generic red variety: stony corals are reef builders, made of polyps that each sit in a cup of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate that the animal secretes as a skeleton [3]. The compendium links the warm pink tones of coral pigments to the red precious corals of the western Pacific, but it found no European sources that use coral as a pigment [3]. Color-name lists use "coral red" only as a hue [1].

The nearest relatives in our name list are [[coral]], [[salmon]], [[vermilion]] and [[orange-red]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 100 paintings, and in 96 by the stricter within-painting measure [4]. Inside a painting it is an accent in 86 per cent of those works [4].

It peaks in the 1400s, in 1.0 per cent of the 945 paintings from that century, about 1.7 times the expected rate [4]. By country it is most over-represented in India, at 3.7 times expected, in 36 of 721 paintings [4]. The earliest match is Bernardo Daddi's [[painting:nga-1|panel of 1333]], which is 553 years before the name's first record in our sources, so it is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph and not proof of coral or any pigment [4]. Look for it as the small red-orange accent in a robe or a lip, not as a background.
